attractions.name: Baltit Fort
attractions.description: A centuries-old fort, former seat of the Mirs of Hunza, with Tibetan-influenced architecture and panoramic valley views.

attractions.name: Attabad Lake
attractions.description: A turquoise lake formed by a 2010 landslide that dammed the Hunza River, now a major boating and photography destination.

attractions.name: Passu Cones & Glacier
attractions.description: Dramatic jagged peaks and glaciers near Passu village, among the most photographed mountain views in Pakistan.

attractions.name: Eagle's Nest Viewpoint (Duikar)
attractions.description: A hilltop viewpoint offering panoramic sunrise/sunset views over Hunza Valley and surrounding peaks.

food_places.name: Karimabad restaurant strip
food_places.specialty: Traditional Hunza cuisine including apricot-based dishes and local walnut cake

seasonal_notes.avg_condition: Mild and pleasant, 15-28°C in valleys, the main tourist season
Crisp and colorful, famous for golden/red foliage in Hunza and nearby valleys
Very cold, heavy snowfall, many high-altitude roads and passes close

travel_tips.tip: Visit Hunza between May and October — many higher areas are snowed in or inaccessible in winter.
A 4x4 jeep is often necessary for side valleys and glacier viewpoints; book local drivers in advance during peak season (July-August).
Roads can be affected by landslides, especially after rain — check current road conditions before travel, particularly along the Karakoram Highway.

history.founded: Historic princely state of Hunza, ruled by the Mir of Hunza until 1974
history.city_history: Hunza was an independent princely state along the ancient Silk Road until it acceded to Pakistan and was formally merged in 1974. It's renowned for dramatic mountain scenery, centuries-old forts, and the longevity of its people.
history.province_history: Gilgit-Baltistan is a mountainous region in northern Pakistan, home to some of the world's highest peaks including K2, Nanga Parbat, and parts of the Karakoram, Himalaya, and Hindu Kush ranges. Historically composed of small princely states (including Hunza and Nagar) along the ancient Silk Road, the region acceded to Pakistan in 1947-48 and is administered separately from Azad Kashmir, with its own Legislative Assembly since 2009.
